paragraphs.text: In a wholly fictional development project, D0 supplies one verified malignant preparation. Drug A asks about a direct repair perturbation: a tumour-only organoid supplies a viable-cell count after 48 hours, with division and death measured separately. The invented exposure series is 0.1, 0.3 and 1 micromoles per litre with three wells per condition and vehicle, positive and mechanism controls. Antibody B instead needs compatible tumour and immune populations over a stipulated seven days, with tumour-only, immune-only, matched antibody or carrier, and recognition controls. B's concentration and schedule are missing. The conventional graft's mouse exposure, schedule, assessment day and controls are also missing, so it remains an incomplete proposal. These conditions are not doses established as safe or achievable in people.

paragraphs.text: A separate fictional three-week decision exercise names real drugs but invents every result. A tumour-only organoid can test a direct olaparib response using an attributed living-cell count after five days; it cannot supply the T cells needed for the pembrolizumab question. Fresh fragments retaining functional resident T cells or a characterised compatible co-culture can address a two-day activation question, with attributed tumour-cell death and recognition controls still needed. A conventional graft cannot restore an intact human immune system and its establishment may miss the deadline. Predicting RNA after BRCA1 loss is a computational hypothesis, not a performed drug exposure. Confirm the actual assay clock: a colorectal six-week median does not forecast the timing for this fictional breast specimen. No choice supplies complete human metabolism, healthy-organ toxicity or every original tumour population.

paragraphs.text: The original model-choice exercise stipulates a fictional virtual-C-v1 model: compatible measured expression data go in, and normalised RNA expression 48 hours after gene C disruption is predicted. No physical drug exposure occurred. Compare unperturbed or no-change baselines with independently measured responses in reserved new donors and the withheld C intervention. All fitting, threshold and preprocessing choices belong to development. A new donor tests a different transfer question from a new perturbation, cell type or laboratory. This computational result can prioritise a measured experiment; it supplies neither protein effects, immune interactions, safe delivery nor clinical benefit.

paragraphs.text: Ladan's real study began with 41 consenting people: three did not undergo biopsy and eight biopsies lacked tumour cells, leaving 30 adequate tumour biopsies. Six assays failed the prespecified baseline-apoptosis criterion and one was lost to infection. Of 23 usable results, three people did not receive the chemotherapy, leaving 20 clinical comparisons. The main-text counts are used here; Table 2's footnote instead mentions two people not receiving chemotherapy. The reported interval for 15/20 agreement was 53 to 89 percent, and the pilot's prespecified target was at least 55 percent. Reaching that target supports further investigation, not a demonstration that using the assay to choose care improves outcomes.

paragraphs.text: The reported breast-study totals imply two sensitive dish calls with sensitive MRI, three sensitive dish calls with intermediate MRI, two intermediate dish calls with sensitive MRI and thirteen intermediate calls matching MRI. Thus 15/20 agree, including thirteen matches in the common intermediate category. Two of four MRI-sensitive tumours were called sensitive in the dish (50 percent), and two of five sensitive dish calls matched MRI sensitivity (40 percent). These are stated comparisons with an imperfect MRI outcome, not validated sensitivity or positive predictive value against known truth. FDA's March 2007 diagnostic-test guidance distinguishes agreement from accuracy when the comparator is not a reference standard. The study's sensitive category required more than 50 percent size reduction after four chemotherapy courses; it is not simply the standard RECIST partial-response category. Usable coverage is 23/30, about 77 percent; a matching clinical comparison was available for 15/30, or 50 percent, including failures and the untreated people in that denominator. Neither ratio measures postoperative benefit.

paragraphs.text: Drug-specific agreement can fail to transfer even within colorectal cancer. Ooft and colleagues reported that organoids predicted the biopsied lesion's response in more than 80 percent of people receiving irinotecan-based treatment, but failed to predict response to fluorouracil plus oxaliplatin. The Netherlands Cancer Institute's 2019 research announcement describes 61 patients in the clinical study; Wensink's later review tabulates 29 people in the response-comparison cohort, including ten receiving irinotecan and twelve receiving an irinotecan doublet. Those cohort and regimen denominators are not interchangeable. This was a prediction comparison, not evidence that assigning treatment by the test improved patient outcomes.

paragraphs.text: Wensink's 2021 review included seventeen publications, five about colorectal cancer; seven used metastatic populations. Its pooled sensitivity was 81 percent and specificity 74 percent for the included response comparisons. The authors warned that these estimates were likely high because some studies lacked quantitative results needed for pooling and not all used a predefined index test; publication or outcome-reporting bias could not be excluded. The pooled establishment estimate was 68.0 percent at patient level and 68.5 percent at sample level, with heterogeneous studies and wide intervals. These are different quantities from response agreement and from clinical utility. The review also reports a 34-day median just to establish organoids from breast biopsies, distinct from a completed drug panel or an individual decision deadline.

paragraphs.text: Vlachogiannis and colleagues studied organoids from heavily pretreated metastatic colorectal and gastroesophageal cancers. They grew organoids from 70 percent of adequately cellular biopsies and compared model and clinical drug responses in 21 comparisons. The reported sensitivity was 100 percent, specificity 93 percent, positive predictive value 88 percent and negative predictive value 100 percent for those comparisons. These are the study's response metrics with its defined comparators and selected denominator, not 88 percent accuracy for all patients or evidence for a postoperative breast decision. Culture success, response agreement and benefit from assigning treatment remain separate questions.

paragraphs.text: Boileve and colleagues prospectively enrolled 87 people with pretreated advanced pancreatic cancer, generated 54 organoids (62 percent) and had 34 evaluable patients with clinical follow-up. The 34 evaluable people are about 39 percent of the original 87, not 39 percent of successful cultures. Mean time to a chemogram was 6.8 weeks; reported sensitivity was 83.3 percent and specificity 92.9 percent. Those selected results and routine-care hit versus nonhit comparisons do not establish a randomised treatment-selection benefit or validate a breast-cancer assay.

paragraphs.text: Read a model study as a sequence of explicitly defined groups: people or specimens offered or submitted, preparations yielding a usable model, results compared with a clinical outcome, and results agreeing under the stated rule. Eligibility exclusions, absent tumour, laboratory failures, missing outcomes and people not receiving the treatment belong to different steps. State whether the unit is a person, specimen or treatment comparison; one person can contribute more than one. A percentage among compared cases cannot describe everyone originally offered testing, and an analysis exclusion is not automatically a failed culture. Keep the drug, cancer, treatment history, outcome, clock and assay version attached rather than ranking different studies as competing accuracy scores.

paragraphs.text: The prospective single-arm SENSOR study enrolled 61 people with metastatic colorectal cancer: 54 were eligible, 31 organoids were generated, 25 cultures were screened against eight drugs and nineteen showed a substantial laboratory response. Six people received an organoid-selected treatment, three vistusertib and three capivasertib, with no objective clinical responses. That observation concerns this panel and selected population; it neither establishes benefit from using the assay nor proves that every organoid method is ineffective. Guillen and colleagues' breast-model report describes a complete response in one person with metastatic triple-negative disease after a model-nominated treatment. That case demonstrates feasibility, without a comparison estimating how often the strategy helps.

paragraphs.text: Randomised outcome evidence must be assessed for the named assay and use rather than declared absent for all functional testing in solid tumours. Ranjan and colleagues reported a 2023 trial of ChemoID selection versus physician choice from the same chemotherapy list in 78 people with recurrent glioblastoma under the 2016 WHO definition. Enrolment stopped after a prespecified efficacy analysis; the intention-to-treat report gave median overall survival of twelve versus 7.5 months. Participants could provide viable tumour through surgery or biopsy, so the findings do not include every patient with recurrent glioblastoma. Cordgenics supported the assay resources, and two authors declared licensed intellectual-property interests. This is evidence for the studied strategy and population, without validating another assay, organoid system, postoperative breast decision or universal treatment rule.

paragraphs.text: The prospective EXALT study tested an image-based single-cell selection approach in 143 people with advanced aggressive blood cancers. Fifty-six were treated according to the assay; 30 of those 56 (54 percent) had progression-free survival at least 1.3 times that on their own previous therapy. The comparator was each person's prior therapy in a single-arm study, not randomised standard care. This result does not show that all tested patients benefited or validate another assay or disease setting. Source: https://doi.org/10.1158/2159-8290.CD-21-0538

paragraphs.text: EXALT used viable material from blood, bone marrow or lymph nodes. These are method- and disease-specific inputs, not evidence that every blood cancer is easy to sample or that its test transfers to a solid-tumour preparation. The 143 enrolled and tested people, 56 receiving assay-guided therapy and 30 meeting the PFS-ratio endpoint remain distinct groups. The comparator for that endpoint was each person's previous therapy; another twenty people formed a physician-choice observational cohort, without random allocation.

paragraphs.text: An original wholly fictional validation exercise uses D0 and its repeated wells only for development, then reserves one pretreatment specimen from each of thirty new donors in an advanced breast-cancer research setting. Lock every fitting, threshold and preprocessing choice before their outcomes. The toy assay counts identified tumour cells after drug A at 0.3 micromoles per litre for 48 hours. Reportability requires malignant identity, calibrated counts, three usable wells per condition, vehicle growth above baseline and the prespecified positive-control response; mechanism results and raw variation remain separate. A treated-count median divided by the vehicle median at or below 0.5 predicts positive, not 50 percent killing. A blinded independent assessor compares the stipulated imaging-volume measurement before treatment and at week six; a decline of at least 20 percent is the invented reference-positive rule, not a clinical response criterion.

paragraphs.text: The fictional locked rule yields twenty reports and ten no-results among thirty donors. Among reportable cases, six are true positive, three false positive, two false negative and nine true negative, using the exercise's assumed-correct reference labels. There are eight reference positives, twelve negatives, nine positive predictions and eleven negative predictions. Correct classifications are 15/20 (75 percent), sensitivity 6/8 (75 percent), specificity 9/12 (75 percent), and positive predictive value 6/9 (about 66.7 percent). Reportable coverage is 20/30 (about 66.7 percent); 15/30 (50 percent) received a correct reportable classification. The ten no-results keep blank predictions, unknown failure reasons and unspecified outcomes, rather than becoming negative or resistant cases. These truth-based toy metrics do not turn an imperfect real MRI comparator into truth or establish clinical utility.

paragraphs.text: Preserve the original prediction and version before measuring an independent outcome, compare against the original rule, then investigate agreement, discordance and failures before developing a revision and testing it on new reserved data. A prospective evaluation fixes its predictions before the corresponding outcomes; retrospective analysis examines material and outcomes already observed. Neither label alone establishes useful care. If the toy team changes v1 after inspecting three false positives, v2 is development and v1's matrix and ten no-results remain unchanged. The later breast-study exercise likewise imagines revising a rule after three sensitive dish calls matched intermediate MRI outcomes; those comparisons are not assumed truth labels. Reusing the same twenty cases evaluates fit to the information used for revision. A move from advanced-disease drug A to postoperative drug B changes intended use again, and improvement during several treatments cannot isolate which treatment helped.

paragraphs.text: Curesponse, based in Rehovot, Israel, and founded in 2018, is the company whose cResponse test keeps a fragment of a patient's tumour alive, with its blood vessels and immune cells intact, to test which treatments it responds to. The test combines ex vivo tumour-fragment culture with rapid genomics and is distributed in the United Kingdom through EDX Medical. Bar and colleagues' 2026 postmarket surveillance report analysed 278 of 312 tested patients, with clinical-response information from 45 survey respondents. Its methods describe exclusions from a treatment-choice analysis, so this proportion is not by itself a culture-establishment success rate. Reported response agreement and changed physician decisions do not establish improved patient outcomes from using the test. OnCo links it to functional ex vivo drug testing and organoid-guided therapy at scale, to the bottleneck of preclinical models that do not predict people, and to ideas on testing drugs on freshly cut slices of the patient's own tumour. Outcome evidence is specific to the assay and intended use; a randomised result for another functional test does not establish benefit from choosing treatment with cResponse. The functional testing page carries the evidence.

paragraphs.text: Izumchenko and colleagues compared 129 treatments across 92 people with advanced solid tumours. Their 112/129 agreement figure (87 percent) grouped stable disease with partial and complete responses as positive disease control; reported sensitivity was 96 percent and specificity 70 percent. Requiring the exact RECIST category instead gave 91/129 agreement (71 percent). Responses came from the consulting oncologist and from xenograft volume changes converted to RECIST equivalents. These selected, repeated treatment comparisons are not 129 independent people, a head-to-head accuracy ranking against other model types or a trial showing benefit from assigning treatment by the model.
